title: Medical roots and suffixes
blurb: Decode medical terms from their roots and suffixes, reading suffix first, use general roots (dict, port, tract) and word-form suffixes, and separate the look-alike endings the HESI A2 tests.
question: A patient's chart mentions gastroenteritis, a planned colostomy and a recent mammogram. Without any medical training, how can you work out what each term means from its parts, and which look-alike endings could mislead you?

teach.h: Medical words are built, not memorized
teach.body: Formally, most medical terms combine a root (often written as a combining form such as cardi/o, with a combining vowel) with a suffix and sometimes a prefix. In plain English: each term is a short sentence in code. The usual reading order is suffix first, then prefix, then root. Hepat/o/megaly reads as 'enlargement' (-megaly) of 'the liver' (hepat): an enlarged liver. Everyday words work the same way: in-spect-ion is the act of looking into.

teach.caption: Starting with the suffix tells you the category first: a condition, a procedure, a person or a record.

teach.h: Word-form suffixes: what job does the word do?
head: Suffix
Makes a
Example
teach.caption: Same root, different job: sterile (adjective), sterility (noun), sterilize (verb), sterilely (adverb).

teach.h: Scenario: Imani reads a lab summary
teach.body: Imani Johnson, applying to a BSN program, shadows on a medical floor. She sees 'hematuria,' 'tachypnea' and 'hepatomegaly.' Suffix first: -uria is a urine condition and hemat is blood, so blood in the urine. -pnea is breathing and tachy- is fast: fast breathing. -megaly is enlargement and hepat is liver: an enlarged liver. Three new words, decoded from parts alone.

teach.text: Classic swaps: -ectomy (remove) vs -otomy (cut into) vs -ostomy (create an opening); -scope (instrument) vs -scopy (procedure) vs -gram (record); -itis vs -osis; -phagia (swallowing) vs -phasia (speech); nephr (kidney) vs neur (nerve); hepat (liver) vs hemat (blood); -logy (the field) vs -logist (the person). Check every part: an option can match the root and still get the suffix wrong.

items: Read suffix first, then prefix, then root.
-itis inflammation; -osis abnormal condition; -emia blood; -uria urine; -penia deficiency.
-ectomy remove; -otomy cut into; -ostomy opening; -plasty repair; -centesis puncture.
-scope instrument; -scopy exam; -gram record; -graphy process of recording.
Body forms: cardi heart, hepat liver, nephr/ren kidney, gastr stomach, oste bone, my muscle.
General roots: dict say, port carry, tract pull, rupt break, vers turn, cred believe; -ist person, -ize verb, -ible adjective.

summary: You can now decode medical and everyday terms by reading the suffix first, then the prefix and root, and use word-form suffixes to tell a person, a thing and an action apart. You can also separate the look-alike endings the HESI A2 tests: -itis/-osis, -ectomy/-otomy/-ostomy and -scope/-scopy/-gram/-graphy.

A.q: After weeks of heavy aspirin use, the patient was diagnosed with gastritis at a clinic visit. Based on its word parts, what does gastritis mean?
A.why: Gastr means stomach and -itis means inflammation: inflammation of the stomach.

whyNot.1: The liver is hepat/o, not gastr/o.

A.why: -ectomy means surgical removal, as in appendectomy.

whyNot.0: -otomy means cutting into (an incision), as in tracheotomy.
whyNot.2: -ostomy means creating a surgical opening, as in colostomy.
whyNot.3: -plasty means surgical repair, as in rhinoplasty.

A.q: Select the word that best completes the sentence: The ____ explained the X-ray results to the patient and her family.
A.why: The blank needs a person who explains. The suffix -logist names a specialist, so a radiologist is the person.

whyNot.0: -logy names the field of study (radiology), not a person.
whyNot.2: -graphy names the process of recording images, not a person.
whyNot.3: -graph names the image or the device, which cannot explain anything.

B.q: Based on its suffix, a "colonoscopy" is
options: an instrument for viewing the colon
an image recorded of the colon
a visual examination of the colon
B.why: -scopy means visual examination, so a colonoscopy is a visual examination of the colon.

whyNot.0: An instrument for viewing is -scope, not -scopy.

B.q: Which term means "enlargement of the liver"?
B.why: Hepat means liver and -megaly means enlargement.

whyNot.2: Nephr means kidney, so this is an enlarged kidney.

B.q: An aide used a wheelchair to transport the patient from his room to the radiology department. Based on its root, what does transport mean?
B.why: trans- means across and the root port means carry, so to transport is to carry from one place to another.

whyNot.0: Pulling is the root tract (traction), not port.
whyNot.2: Sending is the root mit or mis (transmit), not port.
whyNot.3: Writing is the root scrib or script (transcribe), not port.

C.q: A patient's chart lists "erythrocytopenia." Based on its word parts, this term means
C.why: Erythr/o means red, cyt/o means cell and -penia means deficiency: a deficiency of red blood cells.

whyNot.2: -penia means deficiency, the opposite of too many.

C.q: Which term describes a surgically created opening in the colon?
C.why: -ostomy means a surgical opening (a 'new mouth'): a colostomy.

whyNot.1: -otomy means cutting into, an incision rather than a lasting opening.

C.q: Based on its word parts, "arteriosclerosis" means
C.why: Arteri/o means artery and -sclerosis means hardening.

whyNot.3: Softening is -malacia, the opposite of hardening.

reteach.title: Read it like a headline
reteach.question: News headlines often say WHAT happened and WHERE. How does a medical term pack the same information?

blocks.body: Think of each term as a tiny headline. The suffix is WHAT happened: inflamed, removed, enlarged, softened. The root is WHERE it happened: stomach, liver, bone. A prefix adds detail: how fast, how much, around or within. 'Hepatomegaly' is the headline 'Enlargement reported in the liver.' Read the WHAT first so you know what kind of story it is.

blocks.text: Two headlines with the same WHERE can tell very different stories: a tracheotomy cuts into the windpipe, while a tracheostomy creates an opening that stays.

explain.body: The root names the body part or substance: cardi heart, hepat liver, nephr/ren kidney, neur nerve, oste bone, my muscle, hem/hemat blood, cyt cell. Read the suffix first, then the root.

test.q: Based on its word parts, a "hepatologist" specializes in the
test.why: Hepat/o means liver and -logist means specialist.

whyNot.0: Blood is hem/o or hemat/o, which looks similar to hepat/o.

explain.body: -itis inflammation, -osis abnormal condition, -algia/-dynia pain, -emia blood condition, -megaly enlargement, -malacia softening, -sclerosis hardening, -stenosis narrowing, -penia deficiency, -pathy disease.

test.q: Based on its word parts, "neuralgia" means
test.why: Neur means nerve and -algia means pain.

whyNot.2: Muscle is my/o (myalgia); neur means nerve.

explain.body: -ectomy removal, -otomy cutting into, -ostomy creating an opening, -plasty repair, -centesis puncture to remove fluid.

test.q: Which term means "surgical repair of the nose"?
test.why: Rhin/o means nose and -plasty means surgical repair.

explain.body: -scope is the instrument, -scopy is the visual examination, -gram is the record or image produced, and -graphy is the process of recording.

explain.caption: Mammography (the process) produces a mammogram (the image).

test.q: Based on its suffix, a "mammogram" is
options: an instrument for viewing the breast
the recorded image of the breast
the process of recording the breast
a visual exam of the breast
test.why: -gram means a record or image: a mammogram is the image produced.

explain.body: Everyday roots work the same way as medical ones: rupt and fract break, port carry, tract pull, dict say, spect look, vers turn, cred believe, chron time.

test.q: The X-ray showed a hairline fracture in the runner's left shin after the marathon. Based on its root, what is a fracture?
test.why: The root fract means break, so a fracture is a break (here, in a bone).

whyNot.0: Twisting relates to the root tort (torsion) or vers (turn), not fract.
whyNot.1: A bruise is a contusion; nothing in fract means bruise.
whyNot.3: Cutting is the root sect (dissect) or the suffix -otomy, not fract.
